title: Photon Bounce: The Greenhouse Effect
subject: earth science
goal: Find out how gases in the air that absorb infrared change how much energy escapes to space and how much comes back to the ground.
materials: two dice (roll for two tokens at once)
steps: Each round, the Sun sends 4 sunlight tokens straight down through the air to the Ground. Sunlight passes through the air. At the Ground, swap each one for an infrared token: the warm ground gives off infrared.
Move each infrared token up one layer at a time. At each air layer, roll the die and use the table below.
An absorbed token is given off again: roll once more. Even, it moves up a layer; odd, it moves down a layer.
A token that reaches Space has escaped: the Recorder counts it, then it goes back in the infrared pile. A token that comes back down to the Ground warms it: count it, and send it up again next round.
Rounds 1-4 are low CO₂; rounds 5-8 are high CO₂. The Recorder writes each round's numbers.

dice.title: At each air layer, roll once
rows: Absorbed, at low or high CO₂. Roll again to see where it goes next.
Low CO₂: passes up a layer. High CO₂: absorbed; roll again.

listen_for: “Greenhouse gases trap sunlight.” Ask: which tokens did the layers absorb, sunlight or infrared?
“The heat is stuck forever.” Absorbed tokens are given off again, up or down.
Comparing rounds by eye. Ask the Recorder for totals at low and at high CO₂.
debrief: Total the class's escaped and returned tokens at low and at high CO₂. What changed? Escaped drops when CO₂ rises, then climbs back as more infrared bounces around: the ground is getting more energy.
Show NOAA's measurements of CO₂ at Mauna Loa (the worksheet's graph). Ask: what does the graph show since 1960, and how does that connect to the game?
sources: The idea is also modeled in PhET Interactive Simulations' Greenhouse Effect (University of Colorado Boulder). The CO₂ values are NOAA's Mauna Loa annual means (gml.noaa.gov). The activity and questions were written for Paper Loop.
